messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Frank is a 66-year-old software engineer, married for over forty years, who came to therapy at his wife’s gentle but persistent urging. He sat forward in the chair, hands resting on his knees, and described a life lived on high alert. He had always known something was different about him, but it was only in the last few months, after a series of small, inexplicable reactions, that the shape of it had begun to clarify.

The event itself had happened more than fifty years ago, in the basement of his childhood home. His father, a man whose moods could shift without warning, had cornered him there. Frank remembered the cold concrete against his bare legs, the smell of damp and furnace oil, and the specific, searing sensation of his father’s hand—hot, flat, and hard—landing on the back of his neck. It wasn’t the worst beating, but it was the one that had lodged itself permanently. The temperature of that hand, the way it felt like a brand on his skin, had become a fixed point in his memory. He could still feel it, sometimes, without warning. A memory that came not as a picture, but as a sudden, full-body flash: the cold floor, the hot palm, the heart pounding in his chest so hard he thought it would break his ribs.

He had learned, over the decades, to manage. As a software engineer, he found comfort in the predictable logic of code, in systems that followed rules. His work environment was controlled, quiet, and solitary. But even there, the vigilance never stopped. He scanned every room he entered, a habit so automatic he no longer noticed he was doing it. He noticed potential weapons everywhere: a letter opener on a desk, a heavy stapler, the sharp edge of a paper cutter in the supply closet. He didn’t think of them as threats in a conscious way; his body simply registered them, catalogued them, before his mind had even caught up. He had come to believe that this was just how the world worked—that danger was always waiting, and that only constant, exhausting watchfulness kept him safe.

The consequences of this vigilance had crept into every corner of his life. He had stopped accepting social invitations years ago. Seeing people he had once enjoyed—colleagues from old projects, neighbors who waved from their driveways—now felt like a burden. He couldn’t relax around them. He was certain they could see something wrong with him, that they could sense he was different, an outsider playing a part. He had come to believe, with a quiet and unshakeable certainty, that people could not be trusted. Not because they were malicious, but because they were unpredictable. And unpredictability was the thing he feared most.

The most difficult consequence, and the one that had finally brought him to therapy, was the toll it had taken on his marriage. He loved his wife, but he had built a wall of avoidance between them. He could not bear to be touched unexpectedly. A hand on his shoulder from behind would make him flinch, his body jerking away before his mind could register it was her. He had started to avoid physical contact altogether, pulling back from hugs, sitting at the far end of the couch. He had also, without really meaning to, begun to avoid looking at his own body. He dressed in the dark, avoided mirrors in the bathroom, and felt a deep, wordless aversion to the sensation of his own skin. He did not know why. He only knew that his body felt like a place where something bad had happened, and that paying attention to it was dangerous.

What frightened him most was the way his body reacted before he could think. A sudden noise, a door closing too hard, and his heart would be racing, his hands cold, before he even knew what had triggered it. He had spent his whole life trying to be in control, to be rational, to keep the world orderly. But his own body had become a source of chaos he could not manage. He came to therapy not because he believed he could change, but because his wife had said, with tears in her eyes, that she missed him. And he realized, with a hollow ache, that he missed himself too. He hoped, more than he dared to admit, that there might be a way to feel safe without having to stay so hidden.
